lessons.name: THE DIVISOR COUNT IS THE PRODUCT OF (e + 1), at m = 3. The kernel walks every d ≤ 3 testing divisibility, and separately multiplies (e + 1) over 3's prime exponents [[3,1]]; they agree at 2. A divisor is an independent choice of exponent between 0 and e at each prime, so the count is a product of ranges — that is the whole reason, and Wave.lean's 37 divisors_of_*_number_* theorems are this identity evaluated 37 times without it. It is also a SPEED law: the walk is O(m), the product is O(number of primes).

lessons.name: THE UNITS SUM TO ZERO, at m = 56. The residues coprime to 56 add to 0 mod 56, because x is a unit exactly when 56 − x is and the two cancel; with 56 > 2 no unit is its own partner, so the pairing is perfect and the sum is forced. Wave.lean carries 37 separate theorems each asserting this zero at one modulus. The exclusion of m = 2 is the hypothesis rather than an inconvenience: there the only unit is 1, it has no distinct partner, and the sum is 1.

lessons.name: CARMICHAEL AT m = 3, IN BOTH HALVES. The closed form gives lambda(3) = 2 — the lcm over 3's prime powers of p^(e−1)(p−1), with 2 the one place the pattern breaks (1, then 2, then 2^(e−2)). FIRST HALF: every one of the 2 units satisfies a^2 = 1, so 2 kills the group. SECOND HALF: the unit 2 has order exactly 2, so the bound is ATTAINED and nothing smaller would do. Together those are the definition of the group's exponent, and that it is attained by a single element is Carmichael's theorem — true here, and not automatic for abelian groups in general. THIS IS ALSO THE SPEED LAW: computing lambda by folding every element's order walks 2 units for up to 3 steps each; killing the group costs log 2 steps per unit and attainment costs ONE walk. Wave.lean's max_unit_order_mod_* family is this number, sealed 37 times without the closed form that generates it.

lessons.name: THE DIVISOR COUNT IS THE PRODUCT OF (e + 1), at m = 11. The kernel walks every d ≤ 11 testing divisibility, and separately multiplies (e + 1) over 11's prime exponents [[11,1]]; they agree at 2. A divisor is an independent choice of exponent between 0 and e at each prime, so the count is a product of ranges — that is the whole reason, and Wave.lean's 37 divisors_of_*_number_* theorems are this identity evaluated 37 times without it. It is also a SPEED law: the walk is O(m), the product is O(number of primes).

lessons.name: THE UNITS SUM TO ZERO, at m = 55. The residues coprime to 55 add to 0 mod 55, because x is a unit exactly when 55 − x is and the two cancel; with 55 > 2 no unit is its own partner, so the pairing is perfect and the sum is forced. Wave.lean carries 37 separate theorems each asserting this zero at one modulus. The exclusion of m = 2 is the hypothesis rather than an inconvenience: there the only unit is 1, it has no distinct partner, and the sum is 1.

lessons.name: CARMICHAEL AT m = 2, IN BOTH HALVES. The closed form gives lambda(2) = 1 — the lcm over 2's prime powers of p^(e−1)(p−1), with 2 the one place the pattern breaks (1, then 2, then 2^(e−2)). FIRST HALF: every one of the 1 units satisfies a^1 = 1, so 1 kills the group. SECOND HALF: the unit 1 has order exactly 1, so the bound is ATTAINED and nothing smaller would do. Together those are the definition of the group's exponent, and that it is attained by a single element is Carmichael's theorem — true here, and not automatic for abelian groups in general. THIS IS ALSO THE SPEED LAW: computing lambda by folding every element's order walks 1 units for up to 2 steps each; killing the group costs log 1 steps per unit and attainment costs ONE walk. Wave.lean's max_unit_order_mod_* family is this number, sealed 37 times without the closed form that generates it.

FIRST HALF: every one of the 24 units satisfies a^12 = 1, so 12 kills the group. SECOND HALF: the unit 2 has order exactly 12, so the bound is ATTAINED and nothing smaller would do. Together those are the definition of the group's exponent, and that it is attained by a single element is Carmichael's theorem — true here, and not automatic for abelian groups in general. THIS IS ALSO THE SPEED LAW: computing lambda by folding every element's order walks 24 units for up to 39 steps each; killing the group costs log 12 steps per unit and attainment costs ONE walk. Wave.lean's max_unit_order_mod_* family is this number, sealed 37 times without the closed form that generates it.

lessons.name: THE DIVISOR COUNT IS THE PRODUCT OF (e + 1), at m = 17. The kernel walks every d ≤ 17 testing divisibility, and separately multiplies (e + 1) over 17's prime exponents [[17,1]]; they agree at 2. A divisor is an independent choice of exponent between 0 and e at each prime, so the count is a product of ranges — that is the whole reason, and Wave.lean's 37 divisors_of_*_number_* theorems are this identity evaluated 37 times without it. It is also a SPEED law: the walk is O(m), the product is O(number of primes).

lessons.name: EULER'S TOTIENT AS A PRODUCT, at m = 40. The units are walked by gcd; the law multiplies p^(e−1)(p−1) over the factorisation. Both give 16. CRT splits the unit group across prime powers, and at p^e the non-units are exactly the multiples of p. Wave.lean seals 25 of these as bare numbers; this generates them, and it turns an O(m log m) walk into an O(sqrt m) product.

Wave.lean seals 25 of these as bare numbers; this generates them, and it turns an O(m log m) walk into an O(sqrt m) product.

lessons.name: THE IDEMPOTENTS NUMBER 2^omega(m), at m = 21. x² = x is walked directly; the law is two raised to the count of DISTINCT primes — 2 here, giving 4. The exponents do not matter, only how many primes there are: an idempotent is a free choice of 0 or 1 in each prime-power component, so the count doubles per prime and is blind to multiplicity. That blindness is the content — it is why 12 and 18 and 24 all have four.

lessons.name: THE NILPOTENTS NUMBER m / rad(m), at m = 32. A residue is nilpotent exactly when every prime of 32 divides it, so the nilpotents are the multiples of the radical 2 and there are 16 of them. The walk searches for a vanishing power; the law divides 32 by the product of its distinct primes. Wave.lean seals 37 of these counts and states none of this.

lessons.name: THE DIVISOR COUNT IS THE PRODUCT OF (e + 1), at m = 31. The kernel walks every d ≤ 31 testing divisibility, and separately multiplies (e + 1) over 31's prime exponents [[31,1]]; they agree at 2. A divisor is an independent choice of exponent between 0 and e at each prime, so the count is a product of ranges — that is the whole reason, and Wave.lean's 37 divisors_of_*_number_* theorems are this identity evaluated 37 times without it. It is also a SPEED law: the walk is O(m), the product is O(number of primes).

lessons.name: THE IDEMPOTENTS NUMBER 2^omega(m), at m = 38. x² = x is walked directly; the law is two raised to the count of DISTINCT primes — 2 here, giving 4. The exponents do not matter, only how many primes there are: an idempotent is a free choice of 0 or 1 in each prime-power component, so the count doubles per prime and is blind to multiplicity. lessons.name: EULER'S TOTIENT AS A PRODUCT, at m = 55. The units are walked by gcd; the law multiplies p^(e−1)(p−1) over the factorisation. Both give 40. CRT splits the unit group across prime powers, and at p^e the non-units are exactly the multiples of p. Wave.lean seals 25 of these as bare numbers; this generates them, and it turns an O(m log m) walk into an O(sqrt m) product.

lessons.name: THE DIVISOR COUNT IS THE PRODUCT OF (e + 1), at m = 50. The kernel walks every d ≤ 50 testing divisibility, and separately multiplies (e + 1) over 50's prime exponents [[2,1],[5,2]]; they agree at 6. A divisor is an independent choice of exponent between 0 and e at each prime, so the count is a product of ranges — that is the whole reason, and Wave.lean's 37 divisors_of_*_number_* theorems are this identity evaluated 37 times without it. It is also a SPEED law: the walk is O(m), the product is O(number of primes).

lessons.name: EULER'S TOTIENT AS A PRODUCT, at m = 21. The units are walked by gcd; the law multiplies p^(e−1)(p−1) over the factorisation. Both give 12. CRT splits the unit group across prime powers, and at p^e the non-units are exactly the multiples of p. Wave.lean seals 25 of these as bare numbers; this generates them, and it turns an O(m log m) walk into an O(sqrt m) product.

lessons.name: THE NILPOTENTS NUMBER m / rad(m), at m = 25. A residue is nilpotent exactly when every prime of 25 divides it, so the nilpotents are the multiples of the radical 5 and there are 5 of them. The walk searches for a vanishing power; the law divides 25 by the product of its distinct primes. Wave.lean seals 37 of these counts and states none of this.

lessons.name: THE DIVISOR COUNT IS THE PRODUCT OF (e + 1), at m = 53. The kernel walks every d ≤ 53 testing divisibility, and separately multiplies (e + 1) over 53's prime exponents [[53,1]]; they agree at 2. A divisor is an independent choice of exponent between 0 and e at each prime, so the count is a product of ranges — that is the whole reason, and Wave.lean's 37 divisors_of_*_number_* theorems are this identity evaluated 37 times without it. It is also a SPEED law: the walk is O(m), the product is O(number of primes).

Wave.lean seals 25 of these as bare numbers; this generates them, and it turns an O(m log m) walk into an O(sqrt m) product.

lessons.name: THE UNITS SUM TO ZERO, at m = 10. The residues coprime to 10 add to 0 mod 10, because x is a unit exactly when 10 − x is and the two cancel; with 10 > 2 no unit is its own partner, so the pairing is perfect and the sum is forced. Wave.lean carries 37 separate theorems each asserting this zero at one modulus. The exclusion of m = 2 is the hypothesis rather than an inconvenience: there the only unit is 1, it has no distinct partner, and the sum is 1.

lessons.name: THE IDEMPOTENTS NUMBER 2^omega(m), at m = 59. x² = x is walked directly; the law is two raised to the count of DISTINCT primes — 1 here, giving 2. The exponents do not matter, only how many primes there are: an idempotent is a free choice of 0 or 1 in each prime-power component, so the count doubles per prime and is blind to multiplicity. That blindness is the content — it is why 12 and 18 and 24 all have four.

lessons.name: CARMICHAEL AT m = 56, IN BOTH HALVES. The closed form gives lambda(56) = 6 — the lcm over 56's prime powers of p^(e−1)(p−1), with 2 the one place the pattern breaks (1, then 2, then 2^(e−2)). FIRST HALF: every one of the 24 units satisfies a^6 = 1, so 6 kills the group. SECOND HALF: the unit 3 has order exactly 6, so the bound is ATTAINED and nothing smaller would do. Together those are the definition of the group's exponent, and that it is attained by a single element is Carmichael's theorem — true here, and not automatic for abelian groups in general. THIS IS ALSO THE SPEED LAW: computing lambda by folding every element's order walks 24 units for up to 56 steps each; killing the group costs log 6 steps per unit and attainment costs ONE walk. Wave.lean's max_unit_order_mod_* family is this number, sealed 37 times without the closed form that generates it.
